title: How Bluetooth Works
topic_proof: Branch Education, How does Bluetooth Work?, ~10M views
sources: Bluetooth SIG core spec summaries via MathWorks Bluetooth Toolbox docs
EverythingRF: How Bluetooth Avoids Wi-Fi Interference (Sep 2026)

scenes.visual: Close-up phone + earbud, dark studio; glowing hop marks between them
t: Your phone and your earbuds are not connected by anything you can see.
Yet they are changing radio channels sixteen hundred times every second.
Why would a wireless link need to do that?

scenes.visual: Phone opens up, exploded: battery, board, Bluetooth chip, antenna highlighted
t: Let's open the phone and find the part that does the talking.
Here is the board, and on it, a small Bluetooth chip.
Next to it sits a thin metal antenna.

scenes.visual: Chip -> antenna; radio waves leave as rings; 2.4 GHz label
t: The chip turns data into an electrical signal.
The antenna sends it out as a radio wave at about two point four gigahertz.
Bluetooth uses frequencies between two thousand four hundred and two thousand four hundred eighty megahertz.

scenes.visual: Signal wave shifting slightly higher/lower for 1 and 0
t: To carry data, the chip nudges the frequency very slightly.
A little higher means a one.
A little lower means a zero.
The receiver in the earbud simply listens for those tiny shifts.

scenes.visual: Crowded band: Wi-Fi router, microwave oven, other devices flooding the same band
t: But this band is crowded.
Wi Fi routers use it.
So do microwave ovens.
So do thousands of other devices.
One fixed channel would be constantly hit by interference.

scenes.visual: 79 vertical channel bars, glowing marker hopping in a pseudo-random pattern; clock 625 microseconds
t: So Bluetooth splits the band into seventy nine channels.
Your phone and earbud jump to a new channel every six hundred twenty five microseconds.
That is about sixteen hundred jumps every second, following a pattern only the two of them know.

scenes.visual: Wi-Fi block lights up on channels, hop pattern skips them (adaptive hopping)
t: If one channel keeps getting blocked, they stop using it.
This is called adaptive frequency hopping.
The devices must keep using at least twenty good channels.

scenes.visual: Phone sends inquiry waves; earbud replies with its address
t: But how do two strangers find each other?
First, your phone sends out an inquiry.
Any device listening answers with its address.
Then the phone pages that address, and the connection forms.

scenes.visual: Two chips exchange a glowing key; lock closes
t: Pairing is a one time handshake.
The two devices agree on a secret key and store it.
Next time, they recognise each other and reconnect automatically.

scenes.visual: Phone at centre, up to 7 devices around (piconet star)
t: One device becomes the leader, and sets the clock and the hopping pattern.
The others follow it.
This group is called a pico net.
A single leader can serve up to seven active devices.

scenes.visual: Three concentric range rings: 100 m, 10 m, 1 m with power labels
t: Range depends on power.
Class one allows a hundred milliwatts, and about a hundred metres in open space.
Class two uses two point five milli watts, which is about ten metres.
Class three uses one milliwatt, which is about one metre.

scenes.visual: BLE: 40 thin channels, 3 highlighted advertising channels, sensor sleeping then pulsing
t: Fitness bands use a lighter version, called Bluetooth Low Energy.
It has forty wider channels.
Three are used only to announce a device.
The radio sleeps most of the time, so a small battery lasts for a very long time.

scenes.visual: Earbud exploded: antenna -> chip -> driver; audio path
t: Back in your earbud, the antenna catches the signal.
The chip decodes it into music.
And the speaker driver turns it into sound you can hear.

scenes.visual: Zoom out to whole phone and earbud; end card
t: So Bluetooth is a fast, quiet conversation, hopping across seventy nine channels.
All of it, inside a chip smaller than your fingernail.
